claims.text: The investigated alloy has composition Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Extended volumetric pulsed laser remelting should be applied immediately after conventional casting.
Post-casting pulsed laser remelting will enhance amorphous retention and thermal stability in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
The conventionally cast alloy is produced at cooling rates of approximately 10^4–10^5 K/s.
The as-cast alloy contains several primary non-eutectic crystalline phases.
The alloy exhibits a multistep crystallization sequence.
Approximately 10 ns laser pulses are suitable for the proposed remelting treatment.
A laser energy density producing a melt depth of approximately 20–40 μm can remelt the entire bulk region when scanned.
The remelted material will rapidly self-quench through heat conduction into the cooler substrate.
Laser remelting will produce a homogenized amorphous matrix throughout the bulk that is free of pre-existing crystalline seeds.
Rapid quenching after laser melting prevents sufficient atomic reorganization for crystalline-phase formation.
Laser remelting eliminates the primary non-eutectic crystalline phases.
Removing pre-existing crystalline nucleation sites delays crystallization during reheating.
Laser treatment will increase the bulk amorphous fraction relative to untreated cast specimens.
Laser treatment will raise the DSC crystallization-onset temperature relative to untreated specimens.
Untreated Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 has a lower crystallization-onset temperature on reheating.
The proposed benefit is bounded to initial cooling rates of approximately 10^4–10^5 K/s.
The proposed benefit is expected when reheating remains approximately 20–30 K below the DSC crystallization-onset temperature.

contradictions.description: A stated melt depth of only 20–40 μm is presented as treatment of the entire bulk and as producing amorphization throughout the volume, without specifying a sufficiently thin specimen, layer-by-layer processing, or another method that would make the treatment volumetric.

Reheating is limited to 20–30 K below the crystallization onset, but the predicted and falsifying outcomes require DSC measurement of the onset itself, which ordinarily requires heating through that temperature.
